title: Meridian Games: should the sequel be free?
client: Meridian Games, a mid-size video game studio
prompt: Our client is about to release the sequel to a successful multiplayer shooter that sold for sixty dollars a copy. Several competitors have gone free-to-play, making money from cosmetic items instead. The product lead wants a recommendation: charge sixty dollars, go free, or something in between.
background: The first game sold three million copies at launch and has half a million monthly players two years on. The sequel cost forty million dollars to build. The studio has never run an in-game store. A live team of thirty would be needed to keep a free game fed with content.

clarifications.a: Maximise lifetime profit of the sequel over four years, with a strong preference for a large, lasting player base.
Comparable free-to-play shooters report two to four dollars per monthly active player per month, from about five percent of players who pay.
Half the first game's buyers came in during a thirty-dollar sale six months after launch.

exhibits.title: Three pricing models, client's four-year projections
exhibits.note: Revenue per player is net of platform fees. Free-to-play revenue comes almost entirely from the five percent who pay.
exhibits.reveal_when: The candidate asks how the options compare on players, revenue, or cost.

exhibits.title: What happened to two comparable titles
rows: Went free after a paid launch
Player count tripled after the switch
Sequel sold well; player base faded in a year
exhibits.reveal_when: The candidate asks about competitors or precedents.

framework_hints: Lifetime value = players × conversion × spend, minus the cost of feeding the game
Player base as the asset: what else does a big audience enable?
Risk: the studio has never run a store
good_answer: Go free-to-play, but stage it: launch at a low price with a store already built, or free with a paid founder's pack, and commit to the live team. Four-year revenue: premium about a hundred and eighty million; free-to-play about the same headline but with a player base seven times larger and a business that keeps earning; the risk is execution, not economics.
historical_outcome: The real studio's peers who switched to free-to-play in that period generally saw player counts multiply and revenue hold or rise; the paid shooter sequels of 2013 mostly faded within a year. Within five years free-to-play with cosmetic sales became the dominant model for multiplayer shooters, and the largest titles earned billions a year from it.
